segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so one day I wake up with double vision. And this was new. And I am not a panicky kind of person in that situation. I am more a kind of lazy, this is probably nothing, let's just see if this lasts a little while, and just wait it out kind of person.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But this didn't go away. And so I went to doctors, wondering, honestly, if it was kind of a brain thing, which it can be if you have double vision. What happened is that eventually I got to an eye doctor, who told me that what was happening was that I had cataracts-- cataracts. And they had gotten to the point where they were intrusive enough that they were refracting light and causing double vision.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now, the bad news about getting cataracts is that it means that you're old. I mean, I knew I was old. I know I sound young-ish on the radio, but I am over 60. I mean, I'm over 65. I mean, I'm 67. OK.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And can I say, once you cross 60, there is just no pretending at all. And I am fine with being old, but this was the first truly old person thing that had happened to me. That is who mostly gets cataracts.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But the good news about cataracts is it's a simple surgery. It takes 10 minutes. You're awake during it. You see some flashing lights, and then, poof, you're done.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And immediately-- this is really the incredible part of it. Immediately, the world looks different. Everything is brighter, literally brighter. More light is getting inside your eyes. And the world is much more blue than it seemed before.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the way they do it, they do one eye at a time. So they do the first eye. And then you walk around for a week with one fixed eye and one unfixed eye. And so you can hold your hand over each eye and you can compare.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And it's like, I had no idea I was misperceiving the world before the surgery. I had no idea I had cataracts. I had no idea I was missing anything.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I mean, it's funny. Six years before this surgery, I'd bought this photograph, this print that I saw online. And then when it arrived, I was really disappointed because I was like, oh, it's so much more blue in the online picture than in real life.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then after the surgery, I took a look at the picture again, and I realized, oh, no, no. It was the same blue. And I guess what happens is our computer screens pump out so much light directly into our eyes that it cuts through the cataracts, and you see more of the real color. But I had no idea that I was seeing a different blue than everybody else.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's like that stoner cliché. Like, when I say something is blue, when I see it as blue, and you say that you see it as blue, are we seeing the same color? There's no way to know. So today on our show, we have stories of people who see a different blue from the rest of us and then who try to get the rest of us to understand what they are seeing-- sometimes very ham-handedly, sometimes going to great, great lengths. Because after all, how do you give somebody else access to inside your brain and really communicate what it feels like and seems like in there?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today, we hear people try. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life, Act One-- Even Though You Know You Shouldn't.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Shaun was told all of his life that he was going to lose his hearing someday. It happened to his dad, his uncle, his grandfather and great-grandfather, and great-aunt. And when his dad lost his hearing, he was accompanied by a pretty nasty amount of tinnitus.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Tinnitus takes different forms. People hear static noise, rushing waves. They hear tones. His dad's version was a loud buzzing sound, like cicadas, that got louder and louder over time. Shaun's dad was a pastor. And as he aged, all this got so bad that he couldn't preach anymore.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And his dad told him, this is my experience. This is basically the way the color blue looks to me. And someday, this is the way that it really might look to you. And so you need to do the things that can protect you from all this.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They're pretty straightforward. If you're genetically predisposed to hearing loss, you can slow it down if you avoid loud sounds and wear earplugs in noisy places. And you're a kid and adults say stuff like this to you, and you think, yeah, maybe.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: I think that my dad had been telling me it so long, but I also didn't fully believe it. When I first really ingested it was after joining my first real garage band.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He was 14 or 15. It was him and a few friends. And from the start, their very first rehearsal together.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: And just everyone just turning up their amps as loud as we could possibly go. And I had my earplugs that my dad had given me that I was supposed to wear. I wore them two seconds, and I was like, this sucks.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: And I threw them away. And then it was just such a joyous feeling of just the pure sound of these terrible-sounding classic rock covers just filling my body. And I can remember after our first rehearsal, my friend lifted up the garage door, and we all went out and laid on his driveway. And I was just like, man, this is amazing.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Amazing, he says, partly because of the music and partly because he was a shy, quiet kid who always had trouble connecting and interacting with other kids. And here he was, playing in a band together with these guys.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: And so it was just this euphoria of feeling like, I'm doing it. I'm making friends, or making music together. And that feeling lasted for a day and a half, two days. And then I realized that my ears felt like there was cotton in them.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: And I started to hear this sound. And I realized that it was my first bit of tinnitus. And I'm feeling like, oh my god, Dad was right. I was really devastated.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And he resolved, next rehearsal, I'll be different. So rehearsal day came.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: And I was like, this time-- I'm going to wear my earplugs this time. I'm going to be able to do it safe.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And again, after a minute, he took them out.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: And then a couple days later, realizing I'd lost more hearing and just feeling so full of regret and shame and anger, and just this real self-hatred-- it feels so dumb because I feel like I had all the information in my very first interaction with it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He basically repeated that pattern for years. So he was a teenager, losing more of his hearing all the time, and he told no one. Kept this from his parents. Didn't admit the truth to them until much, much later, when he was an adult.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is why I was so interested in talking to Sean. He's somebody who fell into this spiral of shame and secrecy like people have with drinking, or gambling, or drugs, or money troubles. But he was just a kid, this introvert, growing up in a church family with a pastor dad, with this growing noise in his head, this constant buzzing in his ears that only he knew about. As a teenager, he would lie in bed at night and try to hear the sound of his own breathing, and realized that he could not, which was so scary.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: And so I would just constantly try to breathe just louder. And it would just be this cycle of, I can't hear the breath. I ruined my ears. And the irreversibility of it, it was just this real feeling that I had done this really grave physical injury to myself. But it really felt secret and shameful.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's so rare to know anything about what your future is going to be and have people that you trust and love telling you exactly what it's going to look like and how you need to handle it. But knowing all that and actually jumping into action, actually doing the thing you're supposed to do, those are very different things. It can take so long to take action. You tell yourself stories to avoid it. Like, Shaun would tell himself, maybe before I get old, they're going to find a cure for this. Some solution is going to drop from the sky to fix it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then when Shaun gets into his 20s, when he turns 23, something interesting happens. He brings a second person into the secret and into his world of denial and magical thinking. He meets his wife, Abigail.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That happens at a party. They write a song together on their first date. They marry three weeks later.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Not long after that, they quit their jobs and hit the road together as a band. It's just the two of them, a folk-punk duo. They're still a band today, The Bengsons. Anyway, here's Abigail.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: Really early on, you just play in these clubs where it's so loud. It's so intense. And then we'd fall out onto the sidewalk. And you would start opening your mouth really wide and tugging on your ears, and looking around. And you'd start snapping in both of your ears.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You're snapping your fingers by your ears?

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: Yeah, back and forth. And I was in love with you. I didn't really ask a lot of questions. I was like, cool, that's the thing he does.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: But I feel like as time went on that I understood that that was a hearing test. And often, what it meant was that we had done damage. And yeah, I feel like we met so young that we were still a little bit nihilistic about it, even, that it felt like, well, if it's going to go away, let's use it up in fire. Let's use it up joyfully. And there's something to that. But we were also reckless together.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They would play these clubs. And Shaun's attitude at the time was, however loud the other musicians had the monitors, they could do. Whatever anybody else did, he could do.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: And I was like, hell, yeah. Of course, you can. So I think it actually felt like being on his side to be anti-earplug, anti-care. It felt like being a good teammate to be on the side of this recklessness. I don't know. When we first fall in love with somebody, it's like, a way to love them is to see it their way and to embrace even the fiction that they're telling themselves.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Also, nobody wants to be the other person's minder. Do you know what I mean? You're not his mom, you know.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: No, I definitely wanted to be sexy and interesting. I was a new wife. Who wants to be that person, like, nagging? Oh, my god. Like, remember-- put in your earplugs, honey.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When you make the kind of choice that Shaun had made as a teenager, to ignore the reality of what he was up against-- at first, when you're little, it's just your choice. As you grow up, it becomes a choice that other people you love get dragged into. And then they have to figure out how they're going to handle it. Abigail says that she understood that Shaun was going to lose his hearing someday. But to talk about this directly and what it would mean in those early years when they were starting off on this adventure-- they were in love, and they were playing music-- it just felt like they would be talking about the end of their lives.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: It was like having a very unsexy conversation about who we'd be when we were close to death or something. And it felt like, well, once your ears reach a certain point, music will be over. And if music is over, who are we? What does that mean? And when you're 23 and you're like, wow, I might be fully deaf when I'm 50, that feels like, well, so when I get to the moon, I might not be able to hear anymore.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But his ears went on. Abigail said that she would have moments all the time where she would think, the speakers are too loud. This is bad. She should say something.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But there were these clubs, and they were the folk band at the rock clubs. Already, they felt like outsiders. Neither of them wanted to be too demanding or uncool or ask for special treatment. So she kept it to herself.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And all through their late 20s and into their early 30s, Shaun's hearing deteriorated. And to give you a sense of what that means, at some point, Shaun created a little audio demonstration of what the world sounds like to him because he wanted Abigail to understand what he was hearing. So he made this for her.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then sometimes, these days, when they're doing a show on stage, he'll do a version of this for the audience in the theater. And basically, he lost the ability to hear high-frequency sounds first. And the ability to hear those sounds was replaced by a hum at the exact same frequencies that he lost.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: So basically, as you lose frequencies, each frequency that you lose becomes part of the noise.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And that noise, that cicada-like humming, it never goes away. So again, he can hear certain frequencies, and those frequencies become part of this permanent humming sound.

segments.text: OK, so let's hear it.

segments.text: OK, so what I'm hearing is there's a buzzing, but your voice is very-- I can still understand every word you're saying pretty easily.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: That's great. Yeah, my voice is low enough that it's not affecting it too much yet. And then as we go on through the years, OK, I'm bringing in more tinnitus. And you'll probably start noticing that some of it's coming out of my microphone now.

segments.text: Oh, yeah. You're harder to understand.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.text: Wow. Shaun, you said you invented this demo first to show Abigail what you're hearing. Abigail, when you first heard it, I mean, you had been with him for years already, and you knew the basic idea of what he was hearing. What was it like to actually hear the demo?

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: It's very stark, just seeing how hard he had to work.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I mean, did you have a feeling of, like, oh, I knew it was bad, but I didn't realize it was this?

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah, I did. I mean, it's like there's another-- this other huge truth, like another animal in the room with us all the time. And he's navigating it often alone.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: It's hard. We both really aren't interested in thinking about it as, isn't that very sad? It's stark. It's a big difference. But hearing your tinnitus is not a demonstration of tragedy. It's just a stark invitation into your experience.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So this is where Shaun understood he was headed. He knew all of this. His hearing was getting worse and worse. It was hard for him to talk to people if Abigail wasn't there, helping and repeating things.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And when she wasn't there, he would pretend to hear what people were saying. He would nod along. And then often he would say something, thinking that he was understanding the conversation. And then everybody would start laughing and saying, I can't believe you said that, because what he said was so inappropriate and off-topic. And he says sometimes he would never actually learn what his mistake was and what they were talking about.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And his solution was right in front of him. He could slow this down. He could wear earplugs. At the shows, he could have them lower the volume of the speakers on stage, which would do less damage to his ears. But still, he could not bring himself to do it. He was 32 years old. And then--

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: And then we became parents.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They became parents, and they had a boy. And they thought that he would probably inherit ears just like Shaun's, because that's how it goes with the men in Shaun's family. And they wanted their son to grow up with an example of somebody dealing with hearing loss in a much more thoughtful way than Shaun was doing it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And they also needed to change for another reason, something that happened their very first night as parents. Their son, Louie, was born with one lung that would not inflate. And he was rushed off in an ambulance from the hospital they were at to a bigger hospital. And Shaun went to the intensive care unit with the baby while Abigail was in a hospital room recovering.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: That also meant I had lost my translator. And now I'm alone with a child who is maybe not going to make it. They said they thought they were going to have to airlift him to another state to have a lung transplant. And all the nurses were talking with me about all this important stuff, and I couldn't hear them. I just could not follow the conversations.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: And I just felt such terrible guilt and shame that I had let this go on so long. And now my child's life might be on the line. And I couldn't hear well enough to be able to help. I really felt like this has to change, and I have to wake up.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: His son's lungs started working. No transplant was needed. He was fine. But it shook up Shaun.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: It does have a little bit of an addict, rock bottom feeling, like I had really ridden this pony as far as far as it would go.

segments.text: And so what did you do as a result?

segments.text: I started wearing earplugs. That was the first thing, is I just started wearing earplugs. I started having it be a main conversation whenever we would start working with people.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: Getting really vocal about stuff that we had been-- that we were scared people would think we weren't cool, or weren't down, or weren't flexible in the music scene, that we were hard to work with because we had these particular needs, special needs.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: To turn the music down, basically.

segments.speaker: Abigail

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In a way, it's the oldest story in the book. Somebody has a baby and then decides now it's time to clean up their act. That was 10 years ago. And I suppose the story could stop there. After all those years, Shaun starts protecting his ears.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But crazily, after going through all that, there was a second thing that Shaun really needed to do to deal with his hearing loss, something that he had been advised to do years before this, and he still would not do it. He wouldn't get hearing aids, for all the reasons you hear people say. He'd seen his father and grandfather get them. And at some chemical level, he was like, I am not ready to be like that. That is the beginning of the end. That is old age.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so when I first sat down with Shaun and Abigail in the studio, they were like people trapped in quicksand with this decision.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: It's been a gentle-- I'd say four years ago. I was like, maybe it is time for hearing aids. And then the year after that, I was like, all right, it's probably hearing aids time. And then last year I was like, maybe we'll get hearing aids this year. And then this year, I'm like, it's time. But no, I haven't. I have not been able to.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When he explained to me how, I have to say I was surprised at the sprawl and variety of daily things that come up and just how important some of them seem. Like, for example, staying up late with his sister on a visit in the kitchen together, having one of those intimate, late-night talks that would have been literally impossible for him before because quiet conversation was the thing that he could not hear.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: The first night you brought your hearing aids home and then we had this moment where-- we live in a studio. So our kids were asleep right there, and we were just trying to talk about the day.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In the past, two kids asleep in the same room, they might try to talk.

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: And I just couldn't. And we would have to text, or I would need her to speak too loudly and a child would wake up.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And best circumstances in those days, Shaun had so much trouble hearing what Abigail was saying.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: In all honesty, I'm not the most patient woman. And I will give up, I'm embarrassed to say. But I'll give up if there's a lot of repetition sometimes.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: It'll be like, oh, honey, you look great. And he won't hear me. And then by the end I'll be like, you look great! My tone will be ferocious, or something that was supposed to be sweet will be frustrated and crappy. And then that night with the hearing aids, we just had this sweet, gentle, easy conversation. And then later, I was like, oh, my god, I can't believe that happened.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Does this make you wish you had done this years ago?

segments.speaker: Shaun
segments.text: Yeah, I do. I do wish I had done this years ago.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They're both learning ASL, preparing for a future that they're now both looking at pretty squarely.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: When you have a lot less hearing, we're going to be great. We're going to be different, but who wants to write the same song over and over again anyway?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Shaun says that one thing that made all this possible was that he said he needed to be able to picture himself with hearing aids, like how he'd still be able to be a musician and function. And that took a while. Sometimes, even when the evidence is right in front of you, it can take some time to adjust.

segments.text: All right. Why don't we close this out with one of The Bengsons' songs?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up-- what's worse, an eye socket full of red-hot coals while a mule kicks your face for hours, or having a baby, or kidney stones, or being shot with a gun? OK, scientists have actually studied this question. Their data in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's program is Your Blue, My Blue.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And yes, counterintuitively, we are naming the program that, and it has nothing at all to do with this week's midterm election results. This is an episode entirely about things that are in your head, and you wonder if you can communicate those things in your head to somebody else who does not live inside your brain. We have arrived at Act Two of our program. Act Two-- Everybody Hurts.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so everyone knows you're not supposed to compare your pain to someone else's pain. Right? No good can come of that. But one of our producers, Ike Sriskandarajah, recently came across this survey that tries to rank physical pain, and specifically, the pain that people get from cluster headaches. Cluster headaches, if you've never heard of these, are sometimes called suicide headaches because the pain is so severe. This survey held special interest for Ike because he gets cluster headaches. Here he is.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: For me, it started in seventh grade. I was sitting at my desk, listening to the teacher, and then suddenly I felt this wave of knockout pain crash directly behind my right eye. I wondered if I was dying. And then it was gone.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: But it wasn't. It kept happening. And it always came in clusters. Usually, a cycle would last six weeks, four to five times a day, 90 minutes at a time, during which the right half of my face goes slack. My legs spasm. Sometimes I'll throw up from the pain.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I've tried a dozen medications, designed my own home remedies, but a lot of times, I just wait till it's gone. And afterwards, I feel hollowed out, a little lonely. I don't know anyone else who this was happening to, and it was hard to explain how painful these attacks were.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Then I saw this study that compared clusters to better-known extreme pain. And I was like, yes. Here's empirical proof that it's this bad. And I wanted to talk to the people in it.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: The way the researchers did this survey is they found some unfortunate people who get cluster headaches and also suffered some other physical pain. Then they asked everyone to score how painful each experience was. The result is a comparable index of the most painful human experiences. In the survey, one experience really jumped out at me. 25 people got shot with a gun and lived to compare. And that's what happened to Erick.

segments.speaker: Erick
segments.text: Well, I mean, there's a very loud report in a closed vehicle, the ear-deafening blast.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: He was sitting in his car, taking apart his gun, and in the middle of telling a joke to his friend when--

segments.speaker: Erick
segments.text: The first clue that I had been hurt wasn't the actual getting shot part. It came after I had started noticing I was actively bleeding.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Erick, may I ask-- and I know this isn't the point of the story, but what was the joke?

segments.speaker: Erick
segments.text: The funniest part about it is to this day-- I've racked my head about it-- I can't remember. But I remember the punchline being the firearm going off.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: He'd shot himself in the thigh. Somehow, miraculously, there was an off-base Army medic in the parking lot. She stabilized the wound until an ambulance arrived. He says it actually didn't hurt so much at first, but then the pain really got going. And Erick, I want to be clear, really felt the pain fully.

segments.speaker: Erick
segments.text: I refused the opiates. I didn't want them. I was already eight years sober at that point in time when I had gotten shot.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Oh, wow. So you had an unmedicated gunshot wound.

segments.speaker: Erick
segments.text: Yeah. They gave me ibuprofen. And that night, I remember screaming that night for help because it was getting unreal.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Erick, on a pain scale-- 0 no pain, 10 being the most-- how bad did it get with the gunshot?

segments.speaker: Erick
segments.text: I would say a 7 or 8.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: OK. 7 or 8 for a gunshot. His cluster headaches start at 7 or 8 and get a lot higher.

segments.speaker: Erick
segments.text: My 7's are usually me grinding my face in with my fist or a rock. This last month, I almost broke my nose, pressing on my face. I could feel the cartilage trying to break.

segments.speaker: Erick
segments.text: Every now and then, I'll go upwards of 10. And I know that I'm hitting 10 because I'm gasping for air, rocking back and forth, and trying to induce a trance because there's nothing that's going to stop it. And when I get to 10, when I know they're coming, I'll get in my car, and I'll go somewhere secluded. I'll get away from everyone, because it's traumatizing.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I get that. You don't want people to see you writhing in pain. And that pain-- one science writer who also gets this kind of headache described the pain as something, quote, "a tourist would take pictures of as a towering monument or a new world wonder." It's just that big, and yet also totally unseen and mostly unknown.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Here's what we do know. Clusters affect about one in 1,000 people. It's about as common as MS or lupus. They think it's caused by a dysfunction in the hypothalamus. That's the body's inner clock.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: For a lot of people, cluster headaches hit like clockwork. They're eerily precise. The most common time for a headache is 2:00 AM every night. And that's true across countries and time zones. The hypothalamus then connects to nerves in your face, causing severe pain around one eye. For Erick--

segments.speaker: Erick
segments.text: It felt like my eye socket was full of red hot coals and a mule was just kicking me in the face repetitively for hours on end.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: So that's his cluster headache pain.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Which pain do you think you can endure for longer?

segments.speaker: Erick
segments.text: The gunshot for sure.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Erick gets six to seven cluster headaches a day. So in other words, it'd be about as painful, maybe even a little easier, for Erick to get shot several times a day than to have his cluster headaches. In the survey, gunshot wounds received an average pain score of 6, versus cluster headaches, which got 9.7.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: But of course, this is a whole survey of human pain, 17 varieties of affliction. What about the other things people say hurt more than anything, like kidney stones? They're in the survey. Gary, he's had them twice. The first time they hit, he couldn't move.

segments.speaker: Gary
segments.text: I would probably have to put that somewhere between a 7 and 8, say 7 and 1/2.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Can I ask you about your cluster headaches?

segments.speaker: Gary
segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: How bad did they get?

segments.speaker: Gary
segments.text: I'll say I've got a 9.5 or a 9.9, but never a 10. And the only reason I never say I have a 10, because I can always think that there's a level where it gets worse.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: In the survey, people who'd had kidney stones and cluster headaches gave kidney stones 6.9 on average. Gallstones, if you're curious, 6.3.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: There's a lot of ways to get hurt in life. I called around and talked to a college football player who had concussions and broken bones, another person with ruptured ovarian cysts, one lady with endometriosis. I talked with a guy who had a toothache so bad he tried to pull his own tooth out. They all said their clusters were worse.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: There's one more kind of pain, of course, that everyone who goes through it seems to describe as the worst pain they have experienced. I'm talking about the pain of childbirth. How's that compared to cluster headaches?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: A coworker who's experienced this pain told me I lost her on this one. Simply asking the question, I lost her. Two others thought bringing it up was sexist, or at the very least deeply insensitive.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Regular listeners of this show may have heard our stories about the well-documented phenomenon of discounting women's pain. And I believe women. Here's Ashley, talking about the early stages of labor. The birth was almost entirely unmedicated.

segments.speaker: Ashley
segments.text: And oh, I felt everything, absolutely everything.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I can see it in your face.

segments.speaker: Ashley
segments.text: Yes. I would put labor, active pushing, as a 9.5 out of 10.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Is 9.5 the moment of crowning?

segments.speaker: Ashley
segments.text: The tear. I would say the tear itself was 9.5.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Ashley has given birth exactly twice and suffered from cluster headaches hundreds of times.

segments.speaker: Ashley
segments.text: Cluster headaches, a different type of pain. And I would still put cluster headaches as a 10 out of 10.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I should say, she says these two things are impossible to compare. One ends with a baby. The other has nothing good about it at all. And it happens all the time.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: But for her, the headaches are worse. To me, this survey seemed useful, but should really come with a user warning. I've learned that there's a time and a place that's appropriate to share the survey results with someone else, especially if it's your wife.

segments.speaker: Emma
segments.text: I will say that when you first introduced the comparison to me, I was nine months pregnant with our second child.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Back then, I thought the timing made a lot of sense. Emma, my wife-- you just heard her-- was pregnant and pretty uncomfortable. And I was having these headaches, also pretty uncomfortable. So I thought, hey, this article is talking about both of us. It seems like something she might want to know about.

segments.speaker: Emma
segments.text: You said, oh, I read this study that cluster headaches are the most painful thing that a person can experience. I don't remember exactly how you compared them to childbirth, like are more painful than childbirth.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Oh my god. I guess I shouldn't have said that.

segments.speaker: Emma
segments.text: It was something just like that. And my reaction was kind of like, oh, OK. And so I was annoyed. I think saying it ranks above childbirth really rubs people the wrong way.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: If you had to rank my response to your pain, 10 being empathetic and 0 being callous, what ranking would you give me?

segments.speaker: Emma
segments.text: I don't really want to put a number on it. I will say that you were an excellent partner in labor. Though I will say, it's true. For many years, responses to illness or whatever else was a little dismissive. I wouldn't have put you at a 10.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Closer to 0 than 10?

segments.speaker: Emma
segments.text: I don't know. Say right down the middle.

segments.speaker: Emma
segments.text: I think we could say-- yeah, I think we could say 5.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: That's the past or right now?

segments.speaker: Emma
segments.text: Now? I think you've gotten better.

segments.speaker: Emma
segments.text: I don't know. Don't make me do this, please.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Let's just agree. If you want someone to empathize with you, don't try to compare your pain with theirs, especially with empirical data backing up that yours is worse. It does not engender any empathy at all.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: But you know who does get it? Other people with cluster headaches. Before this story, I'd never talked to any. Meeting them meant more to me than I expected.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: One of the first I talked to was a retired New York City firefighter who got his first cluster attack right after 9/11. We compared notes-- how long it took to figure out what was happening, how long before we learned that oxygen really works-- for us, anyway. I just got my first tank this year. He figured it out early. Helps if you work in a fire station and are surrounded by the stuff.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: After our conversation, he gave me a hug and told me, I know your pain. And he did. It felt like empathy on a molecular level. I don't have anything to compare it to.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Ike Sriskandarajah is one of the producers of our show. Act Three-- I'm Blue, Da Be Dee, My Mom Died.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So when we were putting together today's show about things in your head that can be hard to get across to other people, it came to all of our attention that our production fellow, the person who comes here to our show for six months to work with us and learn what we do, Molly Marcello, had something like this herself. She had this thing in her head that was very different from what was in other people's heads, and it was not so clear to her how to handle it. Here she is.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: When I started working here, meeting all these nice, new coworkers, they all had so many questions. And no matter what anyone asked me, my brain only had one answer-- my mom died.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: What stories do you like to cover? My mom is dead. How are you liking New York? Well, my mom is no longer here. What do you think you'll do after this fellowship? I combed the front and back of my hair today. For reference, Mom is dead.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: I find myself constantly rooting around for a second answer. Got any weekend plans? Weekends are good. Communicating can be like offering up a dusty tampon at the bottom of my bag when I was asked for a stick of gum.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: My mom died suddenly three months before I started my job, on a Monday in October-- a perfectly ordinary day to make an exit. At her moment of death, I imagine her saying her favorite word, "shit." It would be nice to know the mechanics of what happened exactly, as if I could just understand the mistake here. Then I could bring it to management, run it up the chain. But sometimes your mother's heart just stops.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: The only time I feel relief from the near-constant interruption of "my mom is dead" is when I get to talk about it. And the only people I like doing that with are other people with dead parents. I was talking with one of them, a coworker here at the show, Mike Comite. He'd mentioned in passing that his dad was dead, and I cornered him about it over lunch one day.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: More people should experience this, Mike said. We laughed because it's such a dark, forbidden thought. We were talking about this impossible gap between what was in our heads and what was in everyone else's when he mentioned this thing that he said had been incredibly helpful to him.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: After his dad died, his friend sent him a zine about grief. Reading the zine was one of the first times it felt like someone understood what he was dealing with, but Mike didn't have it anymore. He'd passed it to an acquaintance of his, someone who'd told Mike how he was going through a big loss too. Months after mailing this guy the zine, Mike found out what the big loss was. The guy's cat had died.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: When Mike told me this story, I said the following out loud-- un-fucking-believable. Then I thought, that's my zine. Mike would have given it to me if he hadn't wasted it on that cat guy. I know that's not exactly generous or kind, or even sensible, but apparently that's the stage of grief I'm in-- the "my dead mom counts more than your dead cat" stage.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: I wanted this goddamn zine, not because I particularly thought it would help me. I'm wary of grief books. If it did, OK, that would be great. But mostly, I needed to right this wrong. Also, it was nice to have a goal. So I set out to get it back.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: Mike agreed to help me in my quest. Unfortunately, he did not remember the title, the author, or most of its content. He couldn't just Google it, so he tried the last place he saw it-- cat guy. Sent a message on my behalf. Hey, remember that zine I sent you a while back? Any chance you held on to it? Crickets.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: We follow up with more emails, social media, LinkedIn. And just like our dead parents, the cat guy gives us no response. Mike then goes back to the person who sent him the zine, and she remembers who wrote it-- Chelsea Granger, an artist who made it in 2019 after her own mom died. We get on the phone.

segments.speaker: Chelsea Granger
segments.text: A few days after she died, I was in my childhood room being like, oh, I'm going to make a zine. There was no question. It starts off with, "My dad called and said my mom is dead."

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: My dad called and said my mom is dead.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Hands-down the most positive I've ever sounded about the worst moment of my life. This was actually kind of thrilling. Chelsea was the first person I'd met whose mom had also died out of nowhere. And that zine she made, she actually ended up making 12 whole months of newsletters about grief.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: Where does the-- OK, where does the newsletter live now? Is it saved on a hard drive?

segments.speaker: Chelsea Granger
segments.text: No. I actually-- I feel like I don't even have scans of it.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: Well, shit. But what Chelsea does have is a folio of her original collages, all in tiny piles, not organized or laid out the way they were in the zine. And incredibly, she offers to resurrect all of the parts, putting them back together from memory, like a 1,000-piece jigsaw puzzle.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: She recreates all 12 months of the newsletter, then copies, staples, and mails them to me. When I have it, I carry it up the steps to my apartment, and the whole thing feels like it's vibrating. Let me open this. Oh, wow. She put the newsletters in this plastic envelope, and they're all stapled. Oh, wow. My heart's beating a little fast.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: What if I hate it? I'm surprised I'm so nervous. I pour everything out onto my bed and start to read. There's printed text alongside handwritten notes, little illustrations, all kinds of stuff-- fragments of other zines, oddball poems, thoughts that friends and readers send in about their experiences of grief. In the March issue, Chelsea draws a thin veil, the kind her mother must be behind. I find this very helpful, to see an image of something I've only felt.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: On a page listing objects that her mother left behind, Chelsea confesses she wears her mom's old, powdery blush. "WTF," she writes. I know, I respond in my head. "WTF. I wear my mom's old mascara. It makes me feel close to her face."

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: In the August newsletter, more recognition. Chelsea writes about how, when her phone rings, she assumes it's someone calling to tell her someone else is dead. I do this too. Every time a friend or relative calls, I let my phone ring at least three, sometimes four times, so I can steady myself for news. I'll just stare at their name a few seconds too long, trying to prepare.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: I finish all 12 months of newsletters in a matter of hours. When I set the last one down, I'm suddenly angry-- furious, actually, pretty much for the first time since my mom died. Because comparing all those notes with Chelsea and her grieving friends, I completely understood what they understood. I felt exactly what they felt, which could only mean one thing. My mom must really be dead too, and I must really be trapped here for good.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: Chelsea writes about how, years after her mother's death, she still conjures her mom in places she's never been. And I realized, of course, I do that too. One time, it almost worked.

segments.speaker: Molly Marcello
segments.text: I was walking down this long subway corridor, composing a text to my mom in my head, when I saw this woman walking towards me wearing these really brightly colored overalls-- white, but patterned all over in psychedelic red, yellow, and green flowers. I was stunned. I had bought my mom the exact same pair just last summer from a random store in Michigan-- only two on the rack and one in my mom's size. She loved them. Made a splash when she wore them to her ladies' poker night. I was so comforted and overwhelmed by those overalls walking toward me that I cried the whole way to Brooklyn.
